title: Why: such acts neither proceed from love of God nor are directed to his glory
source_text: XII. Quod enim actiones hominis peccatoris sine Christi gratia factae, quamvis ex suo genere, & secundum operis materiam bonae sint, revera tamen, secundum Protestantium doctrinam, rationem peccati habeant, causa est, quia neque ex Dei amore procedunt, neque ad Dei gloriam diriguntur. Utrumque enim ad opus quodlibet vere bonum, & Dei judicio tale, plane necessarium putant: neutrum vero in homine Lapso sine gratia Christi salutifera locum habere posse existimant.
pass_a_gloss: XII. For that the actions of a sinful man done without Christ's grace, although by their kind, and according to the matter of the work they be good, yet in truth, according to the Protestants' doctrine, have the character of sin, the cause is, because neither from the love of God do they proceed, nor to the glory of God are they directed. For both for any work truly good, and such by God's judgement, they think plainly necessary: but neither in fallen man without the saving grace of Christ they judge can have place.
pass_b_english: Thesis XII. The reason why, on Protestant doctrine, the acts of a sinner done without the grace of Christ really have the character of sin, though they are good in their kind and as to the matter of the work, is that they neither proceed from the love of God nor are directed to his glory.

The Protestants hold that both of these are plainly necessary for any work that is truly good and good in God's judgement, and they consider that neither can be found in fallen man without the saving grace of Christ.

choices.why: The scholastic language of directing an act to its end; 'refer' keeps the technical sense used throughout these theses.
